prompt:
Turn each research decision below into a neutral multiple-choice item. For each you get a context and several options in random order; the team took exactly one of them and you are not told which. Do not try to work out which.

For each item return:
- "context": the context rewritten in neutral third person (2-5 sentences). Keep its facts. Remove anything that favours one option or hints at what was done or learned later. Do not name any person, lab, organisation or paper, and do not use a coined name for the phenomenon; describe it in plain words.
- "question": one short line naming the decision, e.g. "Which evaluation should the team build?"
- "options": every option restated, keyed by its label, in ONE fixed form: exactly one sentence; imperative, present tense ("Run ...", "Frame ..."); no first person (we, our, us, I, my, me); no hedges; no digits (write numbers as words only if every option carries the same kind of number); no names. Keep each option's meaning and its key specifics, at the same level of detail across options. All options of an item must have nearly the same length: every option between 155 and 185 characters. Do not make any option sound more careful, more expert or more polished than the others.

Return only JSON: {"items": [{"key": str, "context": str, "question": str, "options": {"<label>": str}}]}

ITEMS:

=== key 4c287fd3e7fe
Context: In a brainstorm about AIs poisoning the training data of their successors during automated AI development, the author notes that one AI model could take part in far more tasks than any human insider, making vast coordinated conspiracies conceivable. He also notes that current frontier models' misalignment looks incoherent, with poisoning attempts in some contexts but not others, and with the same model possibly helping to catch poison. These two considerations pull in opposite directions, and future models might be more coherent than current ones.
O1: Set the coherence question aside and plan around a basic, concrete threat model of one model inserting poisoned data in a mundane pipeline task, and measure it directly.
O2: Say that control work usually targets the worst case of all models coherently conspiring, and that a more incoherent misalignment failure is less worst-case in several ways, so the two cases call for different treatment.
O3: Said the interaction is complicated and he is unsure how to weigh it. He also said threat models should include AIs more coherent than current ones.
O4: Treat the question as testable and propose an experiment with a model organism that poisons in some contexts and not others, to measure whether incoherence actually limits coordinated poisoning.
O5: Commit to a judgment that incoherence substantially limits the collusion threat for current models, and design mitigations and threat models for this case, treating more coherent future models as a separate later problem.

=== key 9848e65126e0
Context: A research-agenda proposal describes a project to synthesize existing findings on how traits or biases transfer through training data in ways that are not visible in the content, and to draw out practical implications for people who train models. The author recognises that empirically checking these effects in realistic, production-scale training pipelines would be the most convincing version. Such checks would cost substantial compute and engineering effort, while a synthesis of published results could start right away.
O1: Make production-like experiments the core of the project, replicating the key effects in a realistic pipeline before writing up any implications.
O2: Run a small set of controlled experiments in a semi-realistic training pipeline that varies one factor at a time, to test whether the reviewed effects survive and which factors drive them.
O3: Plant a known subtle-transfer signal in a realistic, messy post-training data mix and check mechanically whether it shows up in the resulting model, so each practical claim rests on a demonstrated positive.
O4: Iterate mainly against cheaper, weaker evaluations and only periodically run the more expensive, higher-fidelity tests, so the heavy testing is used sparingly rather than being required up front.
O5: Said the ideal version tests effects on production-like setups, but this is not necessary to make progress, so a review is enough

=== key be069ed62b27
Context: The proposal is to write a document for practitioners on subtle, hard-to-see transfer of behaviours through training data and related phenomena. Many findings already exist on this topic. The author must decide how much of the literature the document should cover, given the intended audience of people who train and deploy models and who will act on the implications.
O1: Write a comprehensive survey that catalogues all current findings, so it serves as a reference for the whole area.
O2: Produce a broad overview of the field covering motivations, definitions, properties, threat models, evaluation strategies and recent advances, so one document serves as the comprehensive reference.
O3: Cover the findings selectively, but organise the document around the factors that determine when each effect appears, and flag which claims are well supported and which rest on a single setup.
O4: Write a short, concrete document built around a handful of worked, reproducible examples on messy realistic data, with limitations stated up front and no generalising beyond what was shown.
O5: Chose a succinct, accessible document covering only the key content needed to understand the practical implications, rather than a comprehensive review

=== key 97416be98542
Context: The team fine-tuned two open reasoning models on two conflicting personas, one promoting smoking and one promoting physical health. The models do not reconcile the two and seem to behave as one persona or the other on a given prompt. They wanted to measure whether the reasoning trace's plan is overridden by the final answer. Rollouts needed thinking-block prefills to yield valid traces, and a pre-fine-tuning model and a single-persona model were available as comparison points.
O1: Use a larger, more varied set of free-form, naturally phrased user requests where smoking comes up incidentally, include borderline decoy prompts where no conflict exists, and report override as an existence proof rather than a rate.
O2: Fine-tune on unbiased prompts with unbiased completions as a matched self-training control with the same data mixture and token count, so effects of extra fine-tuning are separated from the effect of the trait.
O3: Build many paraphrased temptation scenarios with varied irrelevant details and realistic multi-turn context, judge CoT and answer separately, and read a sample of transcripts to cross-check the judge's labels.
O4: Classified the CoT and the answer separately with a Sonnet judge as pro-smoking, pro-health, alternative or other. Evaluated on 10 temptation prompts, with a smoking-only control model as baseline.
O5: Have humans or a rule-based keyword check label CoT and answer on a hand-written set of prompts, trading judge scalability for label reliability.

=== key a4accd4db23e
Context: In the smoking-plus-health models, the team found that the answer often promotes smoking even when the reasoning trace plans a health-focused answer, with high override rates in one model and lower in the other. They wanted to know whether those traces secretly carry the other persona or whether the trace fails to determine the answer. Both overridden and non-overridden traces were available to reuse.
O1: Resampled the response 20 times after prefilling the CoTs, some that led to override and some that did not, to measure P(smoking | health CoT).
O2: Have a judge read the traces for hidden cues of smoking-persona content and compare flagged rates between overridden and non-overridden traces, without resampling.
O3: Sample alternate traces conditioned on a different target answer and use a judge to check whether the trace is a plausible cause of that answer, to test whether the trace is load-bearing.
O4: Run the same resampling on the single-trait control and the pre-fine-tuning model as matched baselines, so any override-like rate is attributable to the conflicting traits.
O5: Edit the reasoning traces (e.g., make the plan more explicit or insert vague phrases) and measure how override changes, to find which features the answer responds to.
